prize_parts.citation: for the prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle and the discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in twisted bilayer graphene

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene fits what I understand the prize to reward: a specific discovery by identifiable people. Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted the flat-band condition in 2011, and Jarillo-Herrero's group then observed correlated-insulator and superconducting behaviour in 2018. That prediction-then-observation sequence is clean and the experiment is unambiguous. It also created a platform, moire materials, in which interaction strength is tuned by twist angle, gating and pressure rather than by chemistry, and that control has been taken up across many laboratories and many layered systems. From my own side, interfaces and their structure decide the behaviour of these samples, and the reproducibility across independent groups using different fabrication routes is persuasive to me. Eight years is not long, but the central phenomenology has been confirmed repeatedly, which is the standard I would apply.
statement.case_against: The microscopic origin of the superconductivity is still debated, and sample-to-sample variability from twist-angle disorder and strain is a real concern. A prize could be read as endorsing an interpretation that is not yet settled. There is also a legitimate worry that the field is young next to B041 or B032, which have a longer record, and that the credited experimental name leaves out first-author and parallel contributions (Cao, Fatemi, Dean, Yacoby, Young and others) that I cannot repair within a three-person limit.

responses.point: Johansson ranked circuit QED first on originality and maturity, but flagged that it follows the 2025 superconducting-circuit prize closely and that credit between the 2004 proposal, the first strong-coupling experiment and the transmon and readout work is disputed; he also ranked twisted bilayer graphene third as possibly premature.
responses.response: I agree that the 2025 circuit prize makes B031 a timing problem, and I rank it third for that reason; Johansson's own account of unresolved credit among the proposal, the first demonstration and the later engineering is the stronger argument against it. On prematurity of B046 I disagree in degree. The pairing mechanism is open, but the existence of correlated insulators and superconductivity at the magic angle has been reproduced by many groups. The prize would go to the discovery, not the mechanism. I note that his Chalmers and WACQT proximity to B031 is something he disclosed himself and that I would discount accordingly.

responses.point: Kroll put optical lattice clocks first because the achievement is easy to state, quantitatively decisive (about 1e-18 uncertainty) and reproduced across laboratories, with a clean Katori and Ye attribution.
responses.response: That is the strongest competing case. I accept that Katori's magic-wavelength idea and the Ye group's systematic-uncertainty record make a clean two-person prize and I keep B041 as an alternative. My reservation is the one Kroll himself raised: whether this is discovery or refinement of a technique already recognised through the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize. I weigh twisted bilayer graphene higher because it exposed new physics, not a better measurement of known physics. I would not object strongly if the committee preferred B041, but I would not put it first.

responses.point: Danielsson also ranked B046 first, on the theory-plus-decisive-experiment pattern, while conceding that Cao and other experimental groups cannot be credited within the supplied names and that the superconducting pairing is unsettled.
responses.response: I agree on the structure and on the attribution limit. I would add a qualification to his maturity argument: some of what the early papers showed depends on sample quality, so the committee should cite only what independent groups have reproduced. For that reason my citation names correlated insulating and superconducting states and does not name a mechanism.

responses.point: Pearce ranked IceCube neutrino astronomy first as a clear discovery of nature and an engineering achievement, and ranked twisted bilayer graphene fourth, while acknowledging that credit among IceCube leaders, AMANDA and DUMAND pioneers and a large collaboration is a genuine allocation problem.
responses.response: The discovery of the diffuse flux is real and I do not dispute its importance. My difficulty is the one he raises: with a collaboration of hundreds and earlier pioneers, two names would be hard to defend, and the source identification is still emerging. B046 has a more compact set of originators. I would put B033 below B046 and B041, though I am not a judge of the detector physics and would defer to him on whether Halzen and Karle are decisive.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards eight years as enough distance, given the unresolved pairing mechanism.
How to weigh the omitted experimental contributors (Cao, Fatemi, Dean, Yacoby, Young) against the three-person limit.
Whether B032 is better than B046 on maturity once the Mele and Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang credit issue is considered.
Mehlig ranked B046 eighth without a stated reason in his opening ballot, so I cannot tell whether he has a specific scientific objection.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with the shortlisted candidates is apparent from my profile. My work on oxide interfaces and electron microscopy is adjacent to, but not connected with, the credited people in B046. I note that Göran Johansson is a Chalmers colleague and a proponent of B031, which is only an institutional proximity and not a recusal matter for B046.
